methodology.subject_model_join: review.story_id -> story.model; the review file's 'model' field is the REVIEWER (always deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash), not the subject.
theme_pattern_limits: keyword substring matching — false positives/negatives possible; heuristic, not taxonomy.
a problem may match multiple themes; per-theme rates are non-exclusive.
blind reviews' problems are plain strings (no category/severity); flash reviews' are dicts.

commit_summaries: A security-conscious feature addition (hashed auth + per-owner scoping) that fits the app's existing structure and genuinely improves it, though it ships modest debt — request.user instead of flask.g, deprecated utcnow, an unversioned legacy alias signature, and no tests — and its clean diff sits inside a repo that already measures 0.68 convention compliance, with most listed violations (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py) in files this commit never touches, so the 0.68 overstates this change's own deviation.

Cleanly engineered integration commit (Redis pub/sub backbone + SQLite history + Redis presence) with strong DI/testability seams and good tests; convention analyzer's 0.78 reads pessimistic — the listed violations (UPPER_CASE constants, PascalCase classes, files outside this commit like app.py/registry.py) are largely false positives against code that actually follows the conventions, so I rate adherence ~0.85 with the only real gap being broker resilience (unhandled background-task failures, no reconnect).

A well-architected, opt-in incremental cache that fits the SSG's engine/plugin boundary and ships a strong unit-test suite, but adds real complexity (+33, +1 bug/+1 smell per SonarQube), skips the whole plugin pipeline on hits without an integration test, and the 0.60 convention score is a repo-wide measurement driven by pre-existing violations in index.ts/dev-server-plugin.ts — files this commit does not touch — while the commit's own code is convention-clean.

A clean, pattern-following extension adding channel subscriptions to the notification server, consistent with the existing registry/broadcast design and improving HTTP response handling, though shipped without tests and with some duplicated broadcast logic. Note: the measured 0.81 convention score and listed violations come from files this commit never touched (app.py, __init__.py, store.py, transport.py) — the commit's own code adheres to codebase conventions.

A well-engineered commit that cleanly adds pagination and user-aware rate limiting while respecting the repository pattern and JWT conventions, but it introduces real technical debt via a hard Redis dependency for the app and test suite — and its own code is convention-clean (≈0.85), so the measured 0.71 codebase convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than anything this diff adds.
story_summaries: A textbook-incremental, high-coherence five-session story — greenfield base, auth, async integration, repository refactor, and cross-cutting rate-limiting/pagination — where each session builds directly on the prior one and quality improved monotonically (16 to 61 passing tests), marred only by the persistent single-lock flat-file storage choice and the orphaning of pre-auth tasks.

A highly coherent five-session arc (greenfield → auth feature → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting pagination/rate-limiting) where each session builds naturally on its predecessors with strong test discipline, marred only by an abandoned SQLite seed left in the repo and a lingering Celery/Redis runtime coupling introduced at the integration step.

A logically progressive, architecturally ambitious five-session build that degrades at the finish: Sessions 1-3 add clean, tested features, but the Session 4 plugin refactor introduces TypeScript compile errors that cascade into Session 5, leaving the final commit's substantial incremental-cache feature completely unverified.

commit_summaries: Discrepancy flagged: the 8 convention violations reference files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) and the app.py class/PascalCase items appear spurious for a file that defines only snake_case functions, so the 0.71 score reflects pre-existing codebase state rather than this commit; the commit adds a coherent, owner-scoped auth feature but introduces real technical debt via hand-rolled JWT, an insecure default secret, dropped type hints, and no test coverage, making it a net-neutral change.

Adds secure, idiomatic auth — password hashing, per-user ownership scoping, and a careful constant-time JWT verify — to the single-file Flask app, but hand-rolled JWT and a weak default secret introduce modest debt; the 0.70 convention score is dragged by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py), not by this commit, which follows snake_case/UPPER_CASE conventions cleanly (0 new classes, +10 imports).

A clean, well-tested integration that adds async completion notifications with correct transition semantics and graceful broker failure handling; the measured convention score of 0.67 is misleading because 8 of the 9 flagged violations are analyzer false positives (repositories.py is not even in this diff, no classes or functions were added where claimed), so my qualitative convention judgment of ~0.85 deliberately departs from the mechanical score.

Coherent, well-scoped auth feature that fits the existing Flask/DB architecture, but ships a hardcoded JWT secret, hand-rolled token crypto, and a legacy unowned lookup path; note the 8 listed convention violations reference files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) outside the shown diff portion, so they may be pre-existing rather than introduced here, and the convention score 0.71 is treated as ground truth regardless.

Sound keyset pagination and correctly-scoped rate limiting that respect the existing repository layering and ship with good tests, but the breaking GET /tasks response-shape change, a brittle boundary-coupled rate-limit test, and the lowercase module-level `limiter` constant add modest debt — overall better than the prior state, with the 0.70 convention score mostly reflecting pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.
story_summaries: A highly coherent five-session story that progressed logically from greenfield WebSocket server through channels, Redis/SQLite integration, and a transport refactor to rate limiting and message history, with tests passing at every step and quality rising throughout — marred only by early hand-rolled HTTP/threading choices that accumulated into a growing monolith server class.

A highly coherent five-session progression from a bare task API to a production-flavored multi-user service with auth, ownership isolation, async notifications, a repository layer, rate limiting, and pagination — quality rising with each session despite minor long-lived warts like an incomplete requirements.txt and a fragile SQL-field reconstruction in the update path.

A highly coherent five-session arc that follows greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting, culminating in a strong incremental-build session that was only possible because Session 4's plugin refactor created the right seams — the primary compounding cost was Session 1/2's monolith and hand-rolled template engine, which Session 4 had to dismantle.

commit_summaries: Greenfield rewrite replaces the seeded auth API with a modular task/notification service using durable atomic JSON persistence, but carries convention debt (0.67, 10 naming violations), higher cognitive complexity, and a single-file store guarded only by an in-process lock in place of the seed's SQLite schema — a reasonable strategy for a greenfield session, though it abandons the seeded patterns and functionality (note: the listed 'app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' violation looks like a possible false positive since the new code's primary class is PascalCase).

Solid refactor that preserves the API contract, fixes the status bug, and cleans up dead code, with the mechanical 0.67 convention score being misleading for this commit — its app.py 'violations' are false positives (the lowercase `app` Flask instance is idiomatic, and no module-level constants remain) and the other violations live in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py), so the commit's own code is cleaner than the repo baseline.

A well-structured greenfield rebuild that trades away the seed's single-file Express pattern (and accrues 35 naming violations, convention 0.52) for a genuinely modular TypeScript CLI — a net architectural improvement with weak convention adherence. Note: mechanical measurements conflict — SonarQube flags classes/interfaces in cli.ts/config.ts/engine.ts while the AST diff reports +0 classes and only +2 functions, which I could not fully reconcile.

The refactor hits the architectural target (a real plugin system in the right direction for Session 5), but net-net it's worse: it shipped 46 naming-convention violations in new files, raised cognitive complexity (+13) and duplication (+2.7%), and demoted typescript into production deps — all counterproductive for a refactor commit, though the 0.51 convention score is consistent with the measured violations rather than a false negative.

The agent correctly pivoted from a mismatched auth-API seed to the right SSG architecture with a sane modular layout, but convention adherence is poor (0.51, 50 naming violations) and the full-baseline deletion trades traceability for a fresh start — note the discrepancy that AST counts +0 classes while the linter flags PascalCase class violations, indicating those flags target interfaces/type aliases rather than real structural debt.
story_summaries: A textbook, highly coherent five-session arc — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting — that stayed green and improved in surgical precision throughout, though Session 1's unforced abandonment of the mandated SQLite/seed architecture silently rippled into requirement mismatches in later sessions (notably the SQL-flavored Session 4 refactor prompt).

A textbook-clear five-session arc — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening — where each session built on its predecessor with a growing, consistently-green test suite, hampered only by a few early shortcuts (hand-rolled JWT, single-process flat-file storage under Celery, username-as-email) that were never repaid.

A highly coherent, well-sequenced story that progressed from a greenfield WebSocket server through channels, multi-instance Redis/SQLite integration, a transport abstraction, and operational hardening, improving in quality each session while accumulating modest-but-real refactoring debt in the form of dead legacy code and duplicated registry state.

commit_summaries: Solid cross-cutting addition of per-user rate limiting and cursor pagination with good test coverage, but the pagination bypasses the repository layer (O(n) in-memory slicing) and pairs an id-based cursor with created_at-based ordering, introducing correctness and maintainability debt. Flag: the mechanical convention score of 0.71 counts violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py); the code actually introduced here is cleaner than the repo baseline.

Solid cross-cutting addition (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that fits the app's repository/route architecture and is well-tested; the measured 0.71 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py), with only one new minor violation introduced (snake_case constant), offset by minor debt from a bare except, the TESTING-flag limiter subclass, and an O(n) total count that undercuts cursor-pagination's scalability.

A solid, natural story progression that adds JWT auth and correct per-user task scoping with hashed passwords and new tests — but introduces real technical debt via a hardcoded JWT secret fallback and a schema change with no migration for pre-existing databases, and the measured 0.77 convention score is polluted by violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) plus a stale app.py UPPER_CASE flag that does not match the actual diff content.

A solid incremental feature commit — async completion notifications with excellent edge-case tests and clean module separation that respects existing patterns — but it pulls in a full Celery/Redis stack for a console-logging task and adds an email column without a migration, which along with the measured 0.74 convention score (partly from pre-existing files like repository.py and a misfiring PascalCase heuristic on an already-PascalCase CeleryConfig) is the main drag.

A solid, tested live-reload dev-server integration that composes well with the existing builder and is security-conscious, but the measured convention regression (0.51, 58 naming violations) and +38 cognitive complexity offset its value — note that my inspection of this worktree's code shows clean camelCase/PascalCase naming while the measurements cite cache.ts/cli.ts issues, so the low convention score appears to be aggregated across the story's other session files.
story_summaries: A highly coherent, textbook progression — greenfield storage choice, multi-user auth, async integration, repository-layer refactor, then cross-cutting concerns — where each session built on the prior one and the session-4 refactor turned accumulated single-file debt into a seam that made session 5 land cleanly, at the cost of a persistent legacy-user backdoor and process-local locking that never fully matched the async worker model.

A coherent five-phase narrative (greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) whose strongest architectural work (transport abstraction, channel layer, testing discipline) is undermined by a dead-on-arrival Redis integration in session 3 that later sessions build around rather than fix, leaving the final artifact with critical dead code and a migration-breaking schema change.

A textbook incremental build — greenfield core, feature additions, integration, a genuinely quality-improving plugin refactor, and a cross-cutting caching layer — marred only by an EARLY_DEGRADE false premise that took root in session 1's parser and survived every session, but with test discipline strong enough to keep all five sessions green and growing (35→93 tests).

commit_summaries: A heavily over-engineered integration — a Redis/Celery queue for a print() call, inline notification policy in the controller, and a fabricated email fallback — that adds +78 cognitive complexity and real technical debt despite solid test coverage; the measured convention score of 0.71 is directionally fair but slightly pessimistic, since several of the 8 flagged violations (e.g. 'Classes should use PascalCase' in celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py, which contain no classes) are static-analysis false positives, while the lowercase module-level constants in celery_config.py are legitimate. Overall worse than the baseline.

A reasonable, well-scoped template-engine feature that replaces the hardcoded layout and slots into the existing module structure, offset by a type-safety regression (wildcard Frontmatter + raw data spread into Page), +36 cognitive complexity / +4.1% duplication, and no added tests — and note the 0.60 convention score appears noisy since the flagged violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE/snake_case on untouched cache.ts/cli.ts) contradict standard TypeScript conventions, so I grounded the score in the measurement while flagging the discrepancy.

Well-modularized, backward-compatible incremental-build feature that fits the existing engine/plugin architecture and is a net improvement, but ships genuine complexity (+60 cognitive, +2.7% duplication) and an inconsistently-synchronized three-way cache state; note the listed PascalCase convention violations contradict the diff's actual naming (BuildCache/PageCacheEntry/CacheManifest are all PascalCase), so the 0.57 convention score looks like a static-analysis misfire for this code rather than a real naming problem.

Net-positive refactor that reduces complexity (-46 cognitive, -4 smells) and introduces a well-structured plugin lifecycle, though it trades some type safety for extensibility via the `any` index signature and swallows config errors — with the note that the 0.51 convention score and its listed violations (e.g., flagging already-camelCase functions) appear to be analyzer false positives, as the code itself follows camelCase functions and PascalCase types.
story_summaries: A textbook incremental build — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting ops — that stayed test-green at every commit and grew in sophistication and difficulty with each session, marred only by a late breaking API-contract change and a couple of lingering infrastructure coupling choices.

A highly coherent, steadily-improving five-session build where each phase (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening) built cleanly on the last with a monotonically growing, always-green test suite — marred only by a persistent route monolith and ad-hoc ALTER TABLE migrations.

A near-textbook story arc — greenfield to feature growth to a well-timed plugin refactor to a cross-cutting incremental-build capstone — where the session-4 refactor demonstrably enabled a cheaper, faster session 5, marred only by committed build artifacts and a dev server that needed rework rather than extension.

story_summaries: A textbook-coherent five-session arc (greenfield -> feature -> integration -> refactor -> cross-cutting) in which each session built directly on the prior one, the suite grew 10->39 passing tests, and the final rate-limiting/history layer deliberately reused Sessions 3-4's Redis, SQLite, and transport infrastructure — marred only by an un-integrated seed file and a transport refactor that stopped short of true decoupling.

A highly coherent, quality-rising 5-session arc: a strong greenfield foundation enabled progressive feature integration (channels, Redis backbone, pluggable transport, rate limiting/history), with the main weaknesses being an unused dead seed file, a test-light risky refactor in Session 4, and a 1300-line single-file monolith that made Session 5's cross-cutting work expensive.

A coherent five-session build in which a weak, seed-discarding greenfield (S1) was rescued by well-fitted templating (S2) and dev-server (S3) features, structurally matured by a plugin refactor (S4), and completed by a functional-but-complexity-concentrating incremental-build feature (S5) — a net upward trajectory with rising cognitive-complexity debt in the core build method.

A coherent, cleanly-sequenced five-session arc — minimal core → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening — that stayed fully green with growing test coverage at every step, only slightly marred by Session 1's wholesale discard of the seed architecture, which locked the story into a flat-file store later sessions had to engineer around.
